cards.b:
In the 1950s and 60s, mainly in the USA, political scientists wanted to make the subject a real science, like physics or economics.

Their focus moved from institutions to the behaviour of people: voters, leaders and groups. The roots go back to the Chicago School of the 1920s under Charles Merriam.

David Easton listed eight "intellectual foundation stones" of behaviouralism. Remember them; UPSC loves this list.

  • Regularities: behaviour shows patterns.
  • Verification: claims must be testable.
  • Techniques: use proper research tools.
  • Quantification: measure where possible.
  • Values: keep facts and values separate.
  • Systematisation: theory and research must link.
  • Pure science: understanding before application.
  • Integration: work with other social sciences.

"Real Voters Take Quick Votes, So Politics Improves"

The first V is Verification and the second is Values. Regularities, Verification, Techniques, Quantification, Values, Systematisation, Pure science, Integration.

Do not just memorise the list. In an answer, group the eight into three ideas: science (regularities, verification, techniques, quantification), theory (systematisation, pure science) and scope (values, integration). This shows you understand the movement, not just its list.

Easton saw politics as a system. Society sends inputs (demands and support). The system turns them into outputs (decisions and policies). Outputs create feedback, which shapes new inputs.

He defined politics as the "authoritative allocation of values" for a society.

Gabriel Almond: structural-functionalism

Every political system performs the same functions, like interest articulation and rule-making, but through different structures.

Almond and Verba: The Civic Culture (1963)

They studied five countries and found three types of political culture: parochial, subject and participant.

Karl Deutsch

He studied politics as communication, with a "cybernetic" model.

• "Science" without relevance. While scholars counted votes, the US faced the Vietnam War, civil rights protests and race riots. Political science had little to say.
  • Status quo bias. By studying "what is", it quietly accepted the existing order.
  • Value-neutrality is a myth. Choosing what to study is itself a value choice.
  • Western bias. Its models fitted the USA but not new countries like India.

Strikingly, the critique came from Easton himself. In his 1969 presidential address to the American Political Science Association, called "The New Revolution in Political Science", he announced post-behaviouralism.

Its two watchwords were relevance and action. Research should address urgent social problems, and scholars have a duty to act on their knowledge.

• Substance over technique. It is better to be vague about an important issue than precise about a trivial one.
  • Values matter. Scholars should openly discuss values.
  • Engage with crisis. Research must address social crisis.
  • Act. Knowledge brings a responsibility to act.
  • Politicise the profession. Academic bodies should take part in public debates.

No. It gave us survey research, election studies and rigorous methods. In India, the CSDS–Lokniti National Election Studies use these tools to study how Indians vote.

Post-behaviouralism did not reject methods. It said methods must serve meaningful questions. Make this point and you will look balanced.

Indian political science took up behavioural methods from the 1960s.

  • The Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS) was founded in Delhi in 1963 by Rajni Kothari.
  • Its Lokniti programme runs the National Election Studies, large surveys of how Indians vote.
  • Kothari's Politics in India (1970) used systems ideas to describe the "Congress system".

But Indian scholars also showed the limits of imported models. Western theories predicted that modernisation would weaken caste. Instead, Rudolph and Rudolph in The Modernity of Tradition (1967) showed caste associations adapting to democracy.

This is a classic post-behavioural point: methods must be fitted to local reality.

cards.h: Why the 1960s survey was a turning point
cards.b:
Behaviouralists wanted proof, not opinion. A famous early test was Paul Lazarsfeld and others, The People's Choice (1944). They studied voters in Erie County, Ohio, during the 1940 US election. They tracked voters month by month through interviews, and found that a voter's social group, such as religion, class and place of residence, strongly shaped the vote. Most people did not change their minds because of the campaign.

Later, The American Voter (1960) by Campbell, Converse, Miller and Stokes added the idea of party identification. It is a long-term attachment to a party, learned early in life. This is a clear example of the behavioural habit of measuring a concept, then testing it with data.

Sharper distinction: behaviouralism is not the same as "no values". Its supporters wanted value-free research. Critics said the choice of what to study is itself a value choice.

  • Behavioural question: why do people vote as they do?
  • Traditional question: what is a good voting system?

Common exam trap: mixing up behaviouralism and post-behaviouralism. The first is about method. The second, after Easton's 1969 address, asks for relevance and action.

How it is asked. Prelims: identify which study or concept belongs to behaviouralism. Mains: "Behaviouralism gave political science rigour but lost relevance." Comment.

"Post-behaviouralism is a continuation of behaviouralism, not a rejection of it." Comment.
"Explain Easton's systems analysis and its limitations."

Tip: always mention that the same scholar, Easton, led both movements. Use the systems diagram in your answer; examiners reward neat diagrams.

Useful anchors: Easton's The Political System (1953) called for general theory; A Systems Analysis of Political Life (1965) set out the model; the 1969 address launched post-behaviouralism. Add Almond and Verba for political culture, then a short critique and the Indian example of CSDS-Lokniti surveys.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements about Easton's eight foundation stones:
1. One of the stones is Quantification, the idea that behaviour should be measured where possible.
2. One of the stones is Revolution, which asks scholars to act on their knowledge.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: Quantification is on the list and means measuring where possible. 2 is false: Revolution is not on the list; acting on knowledge is a post-behaviouralist credo.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Almond and Verba, in The Civic Culture (1963), studied five countries.
2. Karl Deutsch treated politics as a structural-functional system.
3. Gabriel Almond's structural-functionalism says every political system performs the same functions through different structures.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: the lesson says five countries. 2 is false: Deutsch studied politics as communication. 3 is true: Almond's definition.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The two watchwords of post-behaviouralism are relevance and action.
2. Easton's 1969 address rejected survey research and statistics altogether.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: relevance and action. 2 is false: post-behaviouralism did not reject methods; it said methods must serve meaningful questions.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Rudolph and Rudolph, in The Modernity of Tradition (1967), showed caste associations adapting to democracy.
2. The Centre for the Study of Developing Societies was founded in Delhi in 1963 by Rajni Kothari.
3. Kothari's Politics in India (1970) rejected systems ideas and used only Western models.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: caste associations adapted to democracy. 2 is true: CSDS was founded in 1963 by Kothari. 3 is false: Kothari used systems ideas to describe the Congress system. Two are correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements about the critique of behaviouralism:
1. The critique said that studying "what is" quietly accepted the existing order.
2. The critique said behaviouralist models fitted new countries like India as well as the USA.
3. The critique said value-neutrality was a fact, because choosing what to study is a neutral act.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: status quo bias. 2 is false: its models fitted the USA but not new countries like India. 3 is false: the critique called value-neutrality a myth, since choosing what to study is a value choice. One is correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Charles Merriam: the Chicago School of the 1920s
2. Karl Deutsch: The Civic Culture (1963)
3. Rajni Kothari: Politics in India (1970)
How many pairs are correctly matched?
quiz.w: 1 is correct: the roots of behaviouralism go to the Chicago School under Merriam. 2 is wrong: The Civic Culture is by Almond and Verba. 3 is correct: Kothari's book. Two are correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following pairs:
1. David Easton: authoritative allocation of values
2. Post-behaviouralism: announced in Easton's 1971 address
3. Rudolph and Rudolph: Politics in India (1970)
How many pairs are correctly matched?
quiz.w: 1 is correct: Easton's definition of politics. 2 is wrong: the address was in 1969. 3 is wrong: Politics in India is Kothari's; Rudolph and Rudolph wrote The Modernity of Tradition. One is correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: Easton's model treats politics as a system, in which outputs create feedback that shapes new inputs.
Statement-II: Easton's 1969 address launched behaviouralism and called for methods to be dropped.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are individually true and Statement-II is the correct explanation of Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are individually true but Statement-II is not the correct explanation of Statement-I
Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false
Statement-I is false but Statement-II is true
quiz.w: Statement-I is true: Easton's systems model has feedback. Statement-II is false: the 1969 address launched post-behaviouralism, which did not reject methods.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is NOT one of the three types of political culture in Almond and Verba's study?
quiz.w: The three types are parochial, subject and participant. Revolutionary is not one of them.

quiz.q:
Arrange these works in chronological order:
1. Easton's The Political System
2. Almond and Verba's The Civic Culture
3. Easton's A Systems Analysis of Political Life
4. Easton's 1969 presidential address
Which one of the following is the correct order?
